NHL Puck Line vs. Moneyline: Is the 1.5-Goal Cushion Worth It?

Published October 9, 2026 · 8 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Bet enough NHL games on the moneyline and you'll eventually run into the same frustrating pattern: a goalie stones a breakaway, a power play goal in the final minute puts the result away, and your favorite wins by two — but you were already going to win the bet on a 1-0 final. The puck line exists because of that gap between "won" and "won comfortably," and it quietly changes the math of almost every NHL wager that involves a clear favorite. The question most bettors never actually work through is when paying extra for that 1.5-goal cushion is a good trade, and when it's just giving the sportsbook a better price for no real benefit.

Why the moneyline is hockey's default bet

NHL games are low-scoring and tightly bunched by nature — a typical final score sits somewhere between 2-1 and 4-2, and a comfortable 5-1 blowout is rare enough that it feels notable when it happens. Because margins are small and goalies can single-handedly erase a mismatch on any given night, the moneyline — simply picking who wins, regardless of margin — carries almost all of the betting volume in this sport. That's a real contrast with football and basketball, where the spread is the default and the moneyline is the afterthought.

The puck line is hockey's answer to that spread, built the same way baseball builds its run line: instead of a number that floats game to game, the margin is fixed at 1.5 goals almost every time, and the price moves instead. If you've read our MLB run line guide, the shape of this will look familiar — fixed number, moving price — but hockey's version comes with its own quirks worth understanding before you use it.

What the puck line is actually selling you

Betting a favorite at -1.5 on the puck line means you need that team to win by two goals or more. Betting the underdog at +1.5 means you win if your team wins outright, or loses by exactly one goal. Both outcomes resolve using the final score after overtime and the shootout, the same as the standard moneyline — see our overtime and shootout betting guide for how that final-score settlement works when a game is tied after 60 minutes.

Because a one-goal margin is the single most common way an NHL game ends, that 1.5-goal line splits outcomes in a very particular way: it strips away every one-goal favorite win and hands it to the underdog bettor instead, while leaving two-goal-or-more wins untouched. The price on each side has to account for exactly how often that one-goal-margin scenario actually happens, which is why puck line pricing can look dramatically different from the moneyline on the same game.

A worked example: the same matchup, two ways

Say a strong home favorite is sitting at -170 on the moneyline against a live underdog at +150. That's a fairly typical number for a good team hosting a mediocre one — not a lock, but a clear lean. Here's roughly how that same matchup might be priced on the puck line:

MarketFavoriteUnderdog
Moneyline-170+150
Puck line (fixed at 1.5)-1.5 (+140)+1.5 (-165)

Look at what flipped: the favorite, who had to pay a steep price just to win outright, now pays out at plus money — because a two-goal-or-better win is a genuinely tougher ask than just winning, even for a good team. The underdog, who got rewarded well for pulling the outright upset, now costs more to back on the puck line, because +1.5 pays off on both an outright win and the extremely common one-goal loss. The number didn't move. The entire adjustment for how big an edge the favorite actually has moved into the price instead — which is exactly the mechanism our vig and break-even guide walks through in more general terms.

When paying for the favorite's cushion makes sense

The favorite's puck line only becomes attractive when you believe the game is more likely to be a comfortable win than a nail-biter — a top team at home against a team that's been getting outshot and outscored on the road, a goalie matchup that's heavily lopsided, or a situation where the underdog is running its backup goaltender on the second half of a back-to-back. In those spots, the plus-money price on -1.5 can actually pay better than laying -170 or -200 on the moneyline for essentially the same read on the game, because you're getting paid extra for a margin you already expect.

Where it goes wrong is betting -1.5 purely because the plus-money number looks friendlier than a juiced moneyline favorite. A team can be the right side of a game and still only win by one, especially once empty-net situations and shootout luck get involved — both of which can turn what looked like a safe two-goal lead back into a one-goal final. The puck line isn't a "better version" of the same bet; it's a genuinely different bet with its own failure mode.

The short version: the puck line pays you for predicting the margin, not just the winner — so it only makes sense when your read on the game is specifically about margin, not just which team is better.

When the underdog's insurance isn't worth the price

The flip side is just as important. Taking +1.5 on an underdog converts a game you think is competitive into a bet with a much higher floor — you win on the upset and on the respectable one-goal loss, which covers a large share of plausible outcomes. That's genuinely valuable with a team that's live to win but more likely to lose a tight one.

It's a worse bet, though, with a true long shot — a team getting run off the ice most nights, facing a dominant opponent at full strength. In that spot the moneyline underdog price already reflects how unlikely the upset is, and adding a goal and a half of cushion doesn't change the fact that a bad team can lose by three or four just as easily as by one. Paying extra juice for insurance you weren't likely to need in the first place is how the plus-money appeal of the puck line underdog quietly becomes a worse version of the moneyline bet you'd have made anyway.

Alternate puck lines: pushing past 1.5

Most books also post alternate puck lines — -2.5, +2.5, even -0.5 or +0.5 for heavily mismatched games — letting you move the margin yourself in exchange for a different price, the same flexibility our NFL alternate lines guide describes for football. A genuine blowout candidate, like a top contender at home against a team playing out the string in a lost season, might offer real plus-money value at -2.5 instead of paying through the nose on the standard 1.5. A pick'em-caliber game might only be worth engaging at the half-goal number, essentially a disguised moneyline bet with slightly different pricing mechanics.

Puck lineWhat it requiresTypical use case
-0.5 / +0.5Functions almost like a moneyline betVery close matchups, pick'em games
-1.5 / +1.5Standard margin, the default on nearly every gameMost games, moderate favorites
-2.5 / +2.5Requires a genuine blowoutLopsided mismatches, tanking opponents, back-to-back fatigue

Mistakes bettors make switching between the two

The most common error is treating the puck line as a discount on the moneyline — grabbing -1.5 at plus money on every favorite without separately asking whether a multi-goal margin is actually likely. The second is the mirror image: loading up on +1.5 underdogs purely because the number "feels safe," without noticing the price has gotten steep enough to erase most of that safety. The third, specific to hockey, is forgetting that empty-net goals late in a game — common when a trailing team pulls its goalie — can flip a settled-looking +1.5 cover into a push-the-wrong-way loss in the final minute, which is worth factoring into any live bet around that line.

Puck line pricing reflects the sportsbook's own model of how often one-goal games happen — it isn't a guaranteed inefficiency to exploit. Treat it as a different bet with a different risk profile, not a shortcut to better odds on the same outcome, and see our responsible gambling resources if betting patterns ever start to feel compulsive rather than recreational.

For more on how fixed-margin pricing works in another sport first, read our MLB run line explainer, or go back to all NHL betting guides.

Frequently asked questions

Does the NHL puck line always sit at 1.5 goals?

It's the standard for the vast majority of games, but books also post alternate puck lines like 2.5 for lopsided matchups or 0.5 for very even ones, letting you choose the margin in exchange for a different price.

Does the puck line include overtime and shootout goals?

Yes. Puck line bets settle using the final score after overtime and the shootout are included, the same way the standard NHL moneyline does.

Is the puck line favorite always plus money?

Not always, but often for moderate-to-heavy favorites, since a two-goal-or-better win is a tougher outcome than simply winning. A truly dominant favorite can still be priced at minus money on -1.5 if books expect blowouts to be common in that matchup.

Why would anyone bet the puck line underdog instead of the moneyline?

Because +1.5 wins on both an outright upset and a close one-goal loss, which covers more of the realistic outcomes for a competitive underdog than the moneyline alone — at the cost of a shorter payout than the moneyline would offer.

Can an empty-net goal change a puck line result?

Yes — a late empty-net goal by the trailing team pulling its goalie can turn what looked like a settled puck line cover into a different final margin, which is a hockey-specific wrinkle worth watching on live puck line bets.
